summary: The English of all five verses is sound and agrees with Rashi and Ibn Ezra on the plain sense. The faults are in the analysis and the rulings: the 5:1 literal line invents a 'to' on בְּרֹא; the sense of אָדָם at 5:1.8 ('mankind') contradicts its gloss and the decisions, and its note misattributes a 'humankind' reading to Ramban; the 5:1 accent notes misdescribe the zaqef and revia; the only listed sense of מֵאָה ('hundredth') was filled in mechanically for cardinal numbers. Rashi on 5:3 is misread (Adam separated from his wife, not 'Scripture spoke of the woman'), Rashi on 5:1 bears on סֵפֶר and is followed, Sforno's comparative is lost, and both Onkelos apparatus notes misstate what the Targum does.

patches.value: this book-of generations-of Adam in-day-of creating God Adam in-likeness-of God made ACC-him
patches.reason: בְּרֹא is a bare infinitive construct bound to בְּיוֹם; it has no ל. 'create-to' suggests a prefix the Hebrew lacks.

value.literal: 'this book-of'; a written account; Rashi: סְפִירַת, an enumeration
'in-day-of creating God Adam'; a temporal clause with an infinitive construct

value.english: he made him in the likeness of God
value.literal: 'in-likeness-of God made ACC-him'; English order is rearranged

patches.reason: The third phrase's literal had the same 'create-to'; the first now names Rashi's reading of סֵפֶר. The English fragments are unchanged.
The gloss and the English give the name 'Adam', as the decisions direct for 5:1–5; sense 2 'man, mankind' contradicts them.

patches.value: no article; the pack parses it as a common noun, but it is read as the name Adam, the man whose line follows (decisions, 5:1–5). Ramban speaks here of 'this Adam who is mentioned' (הָאָדָם הַזֶּה הַנִּזְכָּר); his remark that the name covers all human kind is on 5:2.
patches.reason: The old note credited Ramban with a 'humankind' reading at 5:1; on this verse Ramban speaks of the individual Adam created from nothing.

value: סֵפֶר תּוֹלְדֹת אָדָם is a construct chain: 'the book of the generations of Adam'. The etnaḥta on אָדָם closes the first half of the verse; within it the zaqef on סֵפֶר sets זֶה סֵפֶר apart from תּוֹלְדֹת אָדָם.
בְּיוֹם בְּרֹא is a temporal construct: the noun יוֹם stands bound to the infinitive בְּרֹא, with אֱלֹהִים as its subject and אָדָם as its object.

In the second half the zaqef on אָדָם divides the creating (בְּיוֹם בְּרֹא אֱלֹהִים אָדָם) from the making (בִּדְמוּת אֱלֹהִים עָשָׂה אֹתוֹ); the revia on בְּיוֹם and the pashta on אֱלֹהִים are lesser divisions within the first part.
בִּדְמוּת אֱלֹהִים is placed before the verb עָשָׂה for emphasis. The silluq falls on אֹתוֹ.
בָּרָא (create) in the first clause and עָשָׂה (make) in the second are two verbs for one act.
patches.reason: The first note said the zaqef on סֵפֶר 'closes the first clause', and the third that the revia 'opens' the second clause and that the pashta divides the creating from the making. Disjunctive accents end a unit; here the zaqef on אָדָם makes the main division of the second half, and revia and pashta subdivide its first part.

value: Onkelos renders אֱלֹהִים, the subject of בְּרֹא, by the divine name יְיָ ('the LORD'), but keeps אֱלֹהִים in בִּדְמוּת אֱלֹהִים; the Hebrew reads אֱלֹהִים in both places.
patches.reason: The line said Onkelos renders ברא by the divine name; the Targum keeps the verb (דִּבְרָא) and replaces its subject.

value.summary: Rashi: זוֹ הִיא סְפִירַת תּוֹלְדוֹת אָדָם, 'this is the enumeration of the generations of Adam': סֵפֶר is a reckoning, a counted list, not a book; and there are many aggadic midrashim on the verse. The English 'record' follows the plain reading; the midrashim do not bear on it.

patches.reason: Rashi's gloss סְפִירָה decides the sense of סֵפֶר, which bears on the English; the translator's own summary concedes this, so the relation is follows, not not-applicable.

value.summary: Radak: on the day He created him He created him in the likeness of an angel (בִּדְמוּת מַלְאָךְ), by the upper soul He put in him, though he afterwards left His commandments, for He created them male and female and the female enticed him as the serpent had enticed her. He takes אֱלֹהִים in בִּדְמוּת אֱלֹהִים of heavenly beings; the English keeps the plain 'God'.

patches.reason: Radak's 'likeness of an angel' is a reading of אֱלֹהִים in this phrase, a real alternative to the English 'God', not a remark off the plain sense; the summary also left out his point about the woman's enticement.

patches.value: parsed in the pack as the common noun אָדָם, 'human', here given as a name to the pair: Ramban, the name covers the whole human kind, all of whom were in the first pair in potential; Radak, the woman too is called אָדָם, since 'let us make אָדָם' (1:26) was said of both.
patches.reason: A learner needs to know that the name given to both man and woman is the common noun 'human', which the English 'Adam' does not show.

patches.value: wayyiqtol of the III-ה verb חָיָה; the final syllable drops in the short form, so וַיְחִי stands for the long יִחְיֶה
patches.reason: חיה is a final-ה (III-ה) root, not a hollow root; 'hollow' names II-ו/י roots such as מות.
The only sense listed for מֵאָה is 3 'hundredth', the ordinal. Here וּמְאַת is the cardinal 'and a hundred', so no listed sense fits and the sense is removed.

patches.value: construct singular מְאַת before שָׁנָה; the number is stated 'thirty and a hundred'. The pack lists only sense 3 'hundredth' (the ordinal), which does not fit this cardinal use, so no sense is given.
patches.reason: The note now explains why the sense is removed.

patches.value: Rashi: up to this point, the hundred and thirty years, Adam had kept apart from his wife (עַד כָּאן פָּרַשׁ מִן הָאִשָּׁה; Bereshit Rabbah). A midrash on the number of years; it does not bear on the plain sense.
patches.reason: פָּרַשׁ מִן הָאִשָּׁה means that Adam separated from the woman, not that Scripture 'spoke of' her up to here.

patches.value: Ibn Ezra: 'he fathered in his likeness, after his image' is said because God gave Adam the power of begetting to bring forth his own likeness, so that his work would resemble that of the One above. It is not said of Cain and Abel, nor are Cain's years or his age at Enoch's birth given, because Abel's name was blotted out, and Cain's too in the flood; Cain's killing is told to show God's justice, who is slow to anger yet punishes in the end (Exod 34:7).
patches.reason: The old summary had the names of both Cain and Abel blotted out 'in the flood'; Ibn Ezra puts only Cain's line in the flood, and also explains why Cain's ages are omitted.

patches.value: Sforno: 'in his likeness, after his image' means that Seth was more righteous than the first sons (מִן הָרִאשׁוֹנִים is comparative), for even Abel did not bring an offering until Cain had done so before him.
patches.reason: מִן הָרִאשׁוֹנִים is a comparative, 'more than the earlier ones'; 'righteous among the earlier ones' loses Sforno's point.

value: Onkelos: וְאוֹלִיד בִּדְמוּתֵהּ דְּדָמֵי לֵהּ, 'he fathered in his likeness, who resembled him': כְּצַלְמוֹ is rendered by the clause דְּדָמֵי לֵהּ, with no word for 'image'. The Targum also puts the hundred first, מְאָה וּתְלָתִין שְׁנִין.
patches.reason: The line called דְּדָמֵי לֵהּ 'a gloss on the preposition'; it renders the whole word כְּצַלְמוֹ.
Sense 3 'hundredth' is ordinal; שְׁמֹנֶה מֵאֹת is the cardinal 'eight hundred'. No listed sense fits.

patches.value: מֵאֹת, plural of מֵאָה: שְׁמֹנֶה מֵאֹת 'eight hundred'. The pack lists only sense 3 'hundredth' (the ordinal), which does not fit, so no sense is given.
patches.reason: The note now explains why the sense is removed.
Sense 3 'hundredth' is ordinal; תְּשַׁע מֵאוֹת is the cardinal 'nine hundred'. No listed sense fits.

patches.value: מֵאוֹת, plural of מֵאָה: תְּשַׁע מֵאוֹת 'nine hundred'. The pack lists only sense 3 'hundredth' (the ordinal), which does not fit, so no sense is given.
patches.reason: The note now explains why the sense is removed.

patches.value: wayyiqtol of the hollow root מות. The short form in context is וַיָּמָת, with the stress drawn back; here, under the silluq, the pausal form וַיָּמֹת keeps the long ō.
patches.reason: The note called וַיָּמֹת the jussive-shaped form; the short (jussive-like) wayyiqtol is וַיָּמָת, and וַיָּמֹת is its pausal form at the end of the verse, which a learner needs to be told.

verdicts.comment: Rashi reads סֵפֶר as an enumeration (סְפִירָה); 'record' carries it.
A midrash (he begot on the day he was created); the plain temporal clause stands.
תּוֹלְדֹת as the sons and grandsons he fathered; 'descendants' agrees.
A midrash on the hundred and thirty years; the ruling's summary is corrected.
The English keeps 'in his likeness, according to his image' as Ibn Ezra explains it.
